FERPA.name: Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act
FERPA.summary: Protects personally identifiable information in student education records (34 CFR Part 99). Vendors may access records only under an exception such as “school official,” under the institution’s direct control.

GLBA.name: Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act Safeguards Rule
GLBA.summary: Requires a written information-security program (risk assessment, MFA, encryption, vendor oversight) for customer financial information, including student financial aid data.

IRS FTI.name: Federal Tax Information
IRS FTI.summary: Tax data received from the IRS (for example through the FAFSA direct data exchange) is subject to strict redisclosure limits under Internal Revenue Code §6103.

ADA/504.name: ADA and Section 504
ADA/504.summary: Disability-rights laws requiring reasonable accommodations. Disability and medical documentation must be kept confidential and separate from other records.

ADA Title II.name: ADA Title II web accessibility rule
ADA Title II.summary: A 2024 DOJ rule adopts WCAG 2.1 AA as the accessibility standard for the web content and course materials of state and local government entities, including public colleges.

Common Rule.name: Common Rule (45 CFR 46)
Common Rule.summary: Federal protections for human research subjects: IRB review, informed consent, and safeguards for identifiable data.

GDPR.name: EU General Data Protection Regulation
GDPR.summary: Applies to personal data of people in the EU/EEA, including international students, applicants, and seafarers: lawful basis, data minimization, and processor agreements.

TCPA.name: Telephone Consumer Protection Act
TCPA.summary: Requires prior consent for automated or prerecorded calls and text messages.

Library Records.name: State library confidentiality laws
Library Records.summary: Most US states make library patron records, including searches and borrowing history, confidential.

HIPAA.name: HIPAA Privacy, Security & Breach Rules
HIPAA.summary: Protect PHI held by covered entities and their business associates. Vendors handling PHI must sign a business associate agreement (BAA), and uses should be limited to the minimum necessary.

42 CFR Part 2.name: Confidentiality of SUD Patient Records
42 CFR Part 2.summary: Stricter-than-HIPAA protection for substance use disorder treatment records from federally assisted programs. Most disclosures need patient consent, and records can’t be used against the patient in legal proceedings without consent or a court order.

Info Blocking.name: 21st Century Cures Act information blocking
Info Blocking.summary: Providers must not unreasonably interfere with patients’ access to, or exchange of, their electronic health information.

Section 1557.name: ACA Section 1557 nondiscrimination
Section 1557.summary: A 2024 HHS rule requires covered health programs to identify and mitigate discrimination risk in patient care decision support tools, including algorithms.

CMS-0057-F.name: CMS Interoperability & Prior Authorization Rule
CMS-0057-F.summary: Requires impacted payers (Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, CHIP, marketplace plans) to shorten prior authorization decisions and build prior authorization APIs, with most API requirements starting in 2027.

Recording Consent.name: State recording-consent laws
Recording Consent.summary: Some states require every party to consent before a conversation is recorded.

CJIS.name: FBI CJIS Security Policy
CJIS.summary: Governs access to criminal justice information (CJI): advanced authentication, encryption, personnel screening, audit logging, and a signed CJIS Security Addendum for any vendor with access.

Public Records.name: State public records laws
Public Records.summary: Set deadlines for releasing government records, and define what must be withheld or redacted.

VAWA.name: VAWA and victim-privacy laws
VAWA.summary: Violence Against Women Act confidentiality provisions and state laws protect identifying information about victims of domestic violence, sexual assault, and stalking.

Juvenile Records.name: Juvenile record confidentiality
Juvenile Records.summary: State laws restrict access to and release of records about juveniles.

28 CFR Part 23.name: Criminal Intelligence Systems Operating Policies
28 CFR Part 23.summary: For federally funded intelligence systems: information may be entered only on reasonable suspicion of criminal activity, and must be reviewed or purged within five years.

Brady/Giglio.name: Brady and Giglio disclosure duties
Brady/Giglio.summary: Prosecutors must disclose evidence favorable to the defense, including information affecting officer credibility. Drafts and AI outputs can be discoverable.

Fourth Amendment.name: Fourth Amendment
Fourth Amendment.summary: Protects against unreasonable searches. Review of seized digital data must stay within the scope of the warrant or consent.

AI Report Laws.name: State AI-in-police-report laws
AI Report Laws.summary: Some states now require police reports drafted with AI assistance to say so, and to retain the AI-generated first draft.

Civil Rights.name: Civil rights law
Civil Rights.summary: Federal and state civil rights laws prohibit discriminatory policing. Tools that concentrate enforcement on protected groups create legal and community-trust risk.

Surveillance Ordinances.name: Local surveillance-technology ordinances
Surveillance Ordinances.summary: In a number of cities, police must get council approval, publish a use policy, and report annually before acquiring surveillance technology.

Biometric Privacy.name: Biometric privacy laws
Biometric Privacy.summary: State laws such as Illinois BIPA, and some local bans, restrict collecting facial geometry and other biometrics, including for facial recognition.

FAL Convention.name: IMO Facilitation Convention
FAL Convention.summary: Since 2024, ports must accept ship clearance information electronically through a maritime single window.

ISPS/MTSA.name: ISPS Code and US MTSA
ISPS/MTSA.summary: Security plans, security officers, access control, and drills for ships and port facilities.

SSI.name: Sensitive Security Information (49 CFR 1520)
SSI.summary: In the US, vessel and facility security plans and related details may be shared only with covered persons who have a need to know.

TWIC.name: Transportation Worker Identification Credential
TWIC.summary: Required in the US for unescorted access to secure areas of MTSA-regulated vessels and facilities.

MLC 2006.name: Maritime Labour Convention
MLC 2006.summary: Seafarers’ rights, including minimum hours of rest and records of work and rest that port state control can inspect.

STCW.name: STCW Convention
STCW.summary: Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping for seafarers, including watchkeeping and rest requirements.

ISM Code.name: International Safety Management Code
ISM Code.summary: Requires a safety management system, including planned maintenance and reporting of non-conformities.

IMO Cyber.name: IMO Resolution MSC.428(98)
IMO Cyber.summary: Cyber risks, including to shipboard operational technology, must be addressed in the ship’s safety management system.

USCG Cyber Rule.name: US Coast Guard cybersecurity rule
USCG Cyber Rule.summary: A 2025 rule requiring US-flagged vessels and MTSA facilities to maintain cybersecurity plans, designate cybersecurity officers, train staff, and report incidents.

EU MRV/ETS.name: EU MRV and Emissions Trading System
EU MRV/ETS.summary: EU monitoring, reporting and verification of ship emissions. Since 2024 shipping is also in the EU ETS, so reported emissions carry a direct carbon cost.

IMO DCS/CII.name: IMO Data Collection System & CII
IMO DCS/CII.summary: Annual fuel-oil consumption reporting and the Carbon Intensity Indicator rating under MARPOL Annex VI.

nodes.label: Higher Education
nodes.summary: Colleges and universities: research, teaching, enrollment, student success, and the offices that support them.

nodes.label: Research & Sponsored Programs
nodes.summary: Funded research, compliance, and human-subjects protection.

nodes.label: Researcher / PI
nodes.summary: Principal investigators running funded research programs.

details.context: PIs preparing NIH or NSF proposals spend weeks assembling a literature review that establishes novelty. Sources include PubMed, discipline repositories, preprints, and the lab’s own publications.
details.problemStatement: Synthesizing hundreds of papers into a well-cited background section is slow, and reviewers, not the team, often find the coverage gaps.

details.description: Deploy a retrieval-augmented agent over a curated corpus (lab library plus licensed databases) that drafts thematic summaries with inline citations and flags contradictory findings.
details.pattern: Retrieval-augmented generation with citation grounding and a human review pass.
signals: The team already keeps a shared reference library (Zotero, EndNote, Mendeley).
Background sections get rewritten from scratch every proposal cycle.
implementationSteps: Export the lab reference library, plus any full texts the institution is licensed to mine, into a document store.
Chunk and embed the papers, keeping DOI and page anchors on every chunk.
Write prompts that require a citation for every claim and refuse unsupported statements.
Pilot on one past proposal and have the PI score coverage and citation accuracy.
keyBlockers: Publisher licenses may prohibit bulk text mining. Check with the library.
A hallucinated citation is disqualifying in peer review, so verification cannot be skipped.
privacyNotes: Published literature carries no student or subject PII.
Keep unpublished data, draft aims, and any human-subjects data out of third-party tools unless the tool is institutionally approved. Pre-publication ideas are also sensitive IP.

details.description: Standardize how the lab screens, tags, and annotates papers so review work compounds across proposals instead of restarting each cycle.
details.pattern: Standard operating procedure and a shared tag taxonomy.
signals: Each postdoc keeps private notes in a different format.
The same papers are re-read for every proposal.
implementationSteps: Agree on a tag taxonomy: method, population, finding, relevance.
Adopt one group library with required annotation fields.
Hold a 30-minute monthly triage session to tag new papers.
keyBlockers: Adoption depends on the PI enforcing it.
Legacy notes need a one-time migration.

details.description: Many key sources are paywalled or exist only as scanned PDFs. Until access and OCR are solved, any automated synthesis will over-represent open-access literature.
signals: Automated searches return only abstracts for a large share of hits.
Older foundational papers are image-only PDFs.
implementationSteps: Inventory which databases the library licenses for text and data mining.
Run OCR on image-only PDFs and spot-check quality.
State the coverage limits in the proposal methodology.
keyBlockers: License negotiations move on library procurement timelines.
OCR handles equations and tables poorly.

nodes.label: Research Administrator
nodes.summary: Department or central staff managing post-award finances and compliance.

details.context: After an award, administrators reconcile spending against budgets and submit periodic financial and effort reports to sponsors.
details.problemStatement: Expenditures live in the ERP and effort lives in spreadsheets, so every report is a manual reconciliation that delays submission.

details.description: A nightly job pulls expenditures by award from the ERP, fills the sponsor report templates, and highlights variances for review.
details.pattern: Batch ETL with templated report generation.
signals: Reports are built by pasting ERP exports into Excel.
Report formats stay the same across periods.
implementationSteps: Map ERP cost objects to sponsor budget categories.
Build a scheduled extract using a read-only service account.
Generate draft reports and a variance summary for the administrator to approve.
keyBlockers: ERP reporting access usually needs a central IT change request.
Budget category mappings differ by sponsor.
privacyNotes: Salary and payroll lines are employee PII. They are not FERPA records, but they need HR-level access controls.
Graduate assistants are both employees and students. Keep their academic records out of payroll extracts.

nodes.label: No System of Record for Effort

details.description: Effort percentages live in personal spreadsheets with no system of record, so they can be neither automated nor audited.
signals: Two spreadsheets disagree about the same person’s effort.
implementationSteps: Designate a system of record for effort, in HR or research administration.
Define who certifies effort and how often.
Backfill the current fiscal year.
keyBlockers: Requires a policy decision from the Office of Sponsored Programs.
Faculty push back on additional certification steps.

nodes.label: IRB Coordinator
nodes.summary: Supports the Institutional Review Board’s review of human-subjects research.

details.context: Submissions arrive incomplete: consent forms are missing, data-security plans are vague, and recruitment materials are absent. Coordinators return them several times before the board ever sees them.
details.problemStatement: Weeks of back-and-forth delay student theses and funded studies, and board meetings are spent on completeness instead of risk.

details.description: An assistant checks a submitted protocol against the IRB checklist and drafts a return memo listing missing or inconsistent items. The coordinator edits and sends it.
details.pattern: Checklist-grounded document review with a human sender.
implementationSteps: Turn the IRB checklist into explicit, testable criteria.
Run the check on 30 past submissions and compare the results to what coordinators actually flagged.
Deploy inside the IRB system so protocols never leave it.
keyBlockers: The model must never make, or appear to make, an approval determination.
privacyNotes: Protocols describe how data will be collected but should not contain participant data. Reject any submission that attaches identifiable data.
Use an institutionally approved model deployment. Unfunded study designs are confidential.

details.description: A short screening questionnaire routes clearly exempt studies to a lightweight path, so full-board capacity goes to higher-risk research.
implementationSteps: Write the decision tree from the Common Rule exemption categories (45 CFR 46.104).
Pilot it with student theses.
Audit a sample of exempt determinations each quarter.
keyBlockers: IRB chair and board buy-in.

nodes.label: Research Using Student Records Lacks Agreements

details.description: Education research often wants grades, enrollment, or LMS data, but there is no standard path for releasing identifiable education records to researchers.
implementationSteps: Create a data-request process jointly owned by the registrar, IR, and the IRB.
Default to de-identified extracts with small-cell suppression.
Use the FERPA studies exception, with a written agreement, only when identifiable data is truly needed.
keyBlockers: Registrar, IR, and IRB each assume one of the others owns this.
privacyNotes: IRB approval alone does not authorize disclosure of education records. FERPA needs student consent, a qualifying exception, or properly de-identified data.
The studies exception (34 CFR 99.31(a)(6)) requires a written agreement that limits use and requires destruction when the study ends.
Instructors studying their own students must separate their teacher role from their researcher role to avoid coercion and unauthorized access.

nodes.label: Teaching & Learning
nodes.summary: Instruction, course design, and academic department operations.

nodes.label: Faculty / Instructor
nodes.summary: Designs and teaches courses and evaluates student work.

nodes.label: Feedback on Student Writing at Scale

details.context: Instructors in large writing-intensive courses give detailed feedback on hundreds of drafts per term, often with TA help of varying quality.
details.problemStatement: Feedback arrives too late to improve the next draft, and grading consistency across sections is uneven.

details.description: An approved AI tool inside the LMS drafts rubric-aligned comments on each submission. The instructor or TA edits them and assigns every grade.
details.pattern: Human-in-the-loop drafting. The AI never grades.
signals: A clear, criterion-based rubric already exists.
implementationSteps: Use only an institutionally approved tool with a signed data agreement.
Load the rubric and exemplar comments. Do not load past students’ graded work.
Tell students in the syllabus how AI is used in feedback.
Spot-check drafted feedback for bias and accuracy each week.
keyBlockers: Depends on an approved tool existing (see the policy gap).
Faculty governance may require a senate-approved AI policy.
privacyNotes: Student submissions and grades are education records.

A vendor processing education records must qualify under FERPA’s school-official exception: it performs an institutional function, stays under the institution’s direct control, and uses records only for that purpose (34 CFR 99.31(a)(1)).
The contract must prohibit the vendor from using student data to train or improve its models, and must require deletion when the contract ends.
Never paste student work into a personal or consumer AI account. That is an unauthorized disclosure.

details.description: Short norming sessions and a shared bank of annotated exemplars make feedback faster and consistent across TAs, with no new technology.
implementationSteps: Hold a 45-minute norming session each term on three sample papers.
Build an exemplar bank at each rubric level.
Maintain a shared comment library in the LMS.
keyBlockers: TA turnover every term.
privacyNotes: Exemplars from real students must be de-identified and used with the student’s written permission, or written by the instructor.

nodes.label: No Approved AI Tool or Policy

details.description: Instructors want AI help but no tool is approved for student data, so they either do without or use consumer tools and create unmanaged FERPA exposure.
implementationSteps: Publish interim guidance: no student PII in unapproved tools.
Route requests through the AI tool vetting process (IT Security & Privacy).
Offer at least one approved option so the risky path isn’t the only path.
keyBlockers: Contract negotiation with vendors.
Needs academic governance to weigh in on instructional use.
privacyNotes: Shadow AI use is the most common real-world FERPA risk here. Fix it by offering a sanctioned option, not only by prohibiting.

details.context: Instructors field repeated emails about grades, missing work, and standing in the course, sometimes from parents.
details.problemStatement: Students learn they are failing too late, and ad-hoc communication creates privacy mistakes.

details.description: The LMS automatically messages a student when an assignment is missing or their grade drops below a threshold, and links to support resources.
implementationSteps: Enable LMS rules for missing submissions and grade thresholds.
Write supportive message templates that link to tutoring and advising.
Send an opt-in weekly digest to the student’s advisor.
keyBlockers: Messages that feel punitive backfire. Test the wording with students.
privacyNotes: Send only through institutional channels (LMS inbox, institutional email) to the student.
Do not send grades to parents without the student’s written consent. FERPA rights belong to the student at the postsecondary level.
Advisors can receive alerts under legitimate educational interest.

details.description: A one-page guide for instructors and TAs: how to share grades, handle parent calls, and return work without exposing records.
implementationSteps: Publish do/don’t guidance with the registrar.
Add it to TA onboarding.
Route parent inquiries to a standard response.
keyBlockers: Reaching adjuncts and TAs.
privacyNotes: Never post grades by name, student ID, or partial SSN. Use the LMS gradebook.
Don’t leave graded work in a public pile, or discuss one student’s grades in front of others.
A parent claiming the student is a tax dependent should be referred to the registrar, who verifies dependency before any disclosure.

nodes.label: Instructional Designer
nodes.summary: Partners with faculty on course design, media, and accessibility.

details.context: Thousands of legacy PDFs, slide decks, and videos in the LMS lack alt text, captions, and proper structure. The 2024 DOJ ADA Title II rule sets WCAG 2.1 AA as the standard for public institutions.
details.problemStatement: Manual remediation cannot keep pace, and students with disabilities wait for accessible versions.

details.description: AI generates draft captions, transcripts, and alt text in bulk. Designers review drafts for complex images such as charts and equations.
implementationSteps: Prioritize the highest-enrollment courses.
Auto-caption, then human-correct technical vocabulary.
Log remediation status per course.
keyBlockers: STEM notation and discipline-specific diagrams still need experts.
privacyNotes: Instructor-created content has no student PII and can be processed freely under the vendor agreement.
Lecture recordings where students are identifiable, by voice, face, or name, can be education records. Process them only with an approved vendor, or edit students out before processing.

details.description: An accessibility checker scans every course shell on a schedule and sends each instructor a prioritized fix list.
implementationSteps: Enable the LMS-integrated checker.
Send scheduled reports to departments.
Track the trend by college.
keyBlockers: Checkers catch only part of WCAG issues. Manual review is still needed.

details.description: Provide accessible slide, syllabus, and document templates, plus short training, so new content is accessible from the start.
implementationSteps: Publish templates with built-in heading structure.
Run 20-minute workshops.
Make templates the default in the course shell.
keyBlockers: Faculty habits.

nodes.label: Department Chair
nodes.summary: Manages course schedules, teaching assignments, and department operations.

details.context: Chairs build next term’s schedule by copying last year’s and adjusting by email, balancing faculty availability, rooms, and student demand.
details.problemStatement: Required courses conflict, sections fill or sit empty, and students’ time to degree grows.

details.description: A constraint solver drafts a schedule from aggregate demand (waitlists, degree-plan projections), room capacity, and faculty constraints.
implementationSteps: Gather aggregate demand by course.
Encode hard and soft constraints.
The chair reviews the draft and resolves conflicts.
keyBlockers: Room and faculty availability data (see gap).
privacyNotes: Use aggregate counts only. The scheduler does not need individual student records.
Faculty availability can reveal medical or family leave. Store only the constraint, never the reason.

details.description: Room features and faculty constraints live in emails and memory, so no tool can schedule reliably.
implementationSteps: Build a room inventory with features.
Collect faculty constraints through a form.
keyBlockers: Facilities and the registrar own different pieces.

details.description: A published scheduling timeline and priority rules, such as required courses first and no conflicts within a cohort, reduce churn.
implementationSteps: Publish the timeline.
Define conflict-free course pairs for each major.
Hold a cross-department conflict check.
keyBlockers: Chairs working in isolation.

nodes.label: Enrollment Management
nodes.summary: Admissions, recruitment, and financial aid.

nodes.label: Admissions Counselor
nodes.summary: Recruits prospective students and evaluates applications.

details.context: Transfer applicants send transcripts from hundreds of institutions, as PDFs, paper scans, or electronic exchange.
details.problemStatement: Manual keying of courses and grades creates a multi-week backlog at peak season, and admitted students enroll elsewhere.

details.description: Document AI extracts institution, courses, credits, and grades into a structured draft that staff verify instead of typing.
details.pattern: Intelligent document processing with confidence-based review.
implementationSteps: Label 200 historical transcripts across top feeder schools.
Measure extraction accuracy per field.
Auto-accept only high-confidence fields and queue the rest for review.
keyBlockers: Low-quality scans reduce accuracy.
privacyNotes: Transcripts contain dates of birth and sometimes SSNs. Configure extraction to drop fields you do not need.

FERPA covers records once the student enrolls. Protect applicant records to the same standard from day one, since they become education records, and state privacy laws, or GDPR for EU applicants, may already apply.

A vendor processing education records must qualify under FERPA’s school-official exception: it performs an institutional function, stays under the institution’s direct control, and uses records only for that purpose (34 CFR 99.31(a)(1)).
The contract must prohibit the vendor from using student data to train or improve its models, and must require deletion when the contract ends.

details.description: Transcripts arriving through an electronic exchange network go straight into the SIS by webhook, with no manual handling.
implementationSteps: Enable the exchange provider’s delivery webhook.
Map the standard transcript schema to SIS fields.
Alert staff only on mapping failures.
keyBlockers: Only some sending institutions use electronic exchange.
privacyNotes: Use authenticated, encrypted endpoints. Do not route transcripts through shared inboxes.
Error alerts should reference an application ID, not course or grade detail.

details.description: Even perfectly extracted courses cannot be evaluated automatically, because equivalencies live in evaluators’ heads and old spreadsheets.
implementationSteps: Consolidate past equivalency decisions into one table.
Assign a faculty owner for each subject.
Publish equivalencies so students can check them themselves.
keyBlockers: Faculty sign-off is slow.
Past decisions are inconsistent.
privacyNotes: Course-to-course equivalencies are not student data and can be published.

details.context: Admissions receives thousands of repetitive questions about deadlines, programs, costs, and visits by email, chat, and phone, peaking at night and on weekends.
details.problemStatement: Slow responses lose prospects, and counselors have no time for applicants who need real guidance.

details.description: A website assistant answers only from published admissions pages and hands off to a counselor for anything application-specific.
implementationSteps: Index public admissions, cost, and program pages.
Refuse application-status questions and redirect them to the authenticated portal.
Review unanswered questions weekly and fix the website.
keyBlockers: Website content must be accurate first.
privacyNotes: Don’t ask for or store personal details in anonymous chat. Status checks belong behind portal login.
Publish a chat privacy notice. Prospects may be minors or EU residents, where GDPR applies.

details.description: Inquiries are auto-assigned to the territory counselor with templated first responses and follow-up tasks.
implementationSteps: Define routing rules by territory and program.
Create response templates.
Track time to first response.
keyBlockers: CRM data hygiene.
privacyNotes: Prospect data is personal information even though FERPA doesn’t apply yet. Honor unsubscribe requests and state privacy rights.
Text messaging requires documented prior consent under the TCPA.

nodes.label: Financial Aid Counselor
nodes.summary: Packages aid and completes federal verification.

details.context: Students selected for verification upload tax documents, household forms, and identity documents. Staff chase missing items and review each file by hand.
details.problemStatement: Verification backlogs delay aid disbursement, and students, disproportionately first-generation and low-income, stop out before aid arrives.

details.description: The student portal shows a live checklist of outstanding documents and sends automated reminders until the file is complete.
implementationSteps: Sync verification requirements from the aid system to the portal.
Schedule reminders by email and portal notification.
Escalate files still incomplete after 14 days to a counselor.
keyBlockers: Aid system integration.
privacyNotes: Reminders say only “you have items outstanding, log in to view.” No dollar amounts, tax details, or document names in email or SMS.
Financial aid data is covered by the GLBA Safeguards Rule as well as FERPA.

details.description: Classify uploaded documents by type and flag obvious mismatches so counselors review only the exceptions. It never decides eligibility.
implementationSteps: Run in the aid vendor’s approved environment or a private deployment.
Classify document type and completeness only.
Counselors keep all verification decisions.
keyBlockers: Few vendors meet GLBA and federal data requirements.
The error cost is high: wrong flags delay aid.
privacyNotes: Federal tax information (FTI) received through the FAFSA direct data exchange is subject to IRS redisclosure restrictions. It must never go to AI tools or systems not approved for FTI.
Student-uploaded tax and identity documents are still GLBA-protected. They require encryption, MFA, and a vendor risk assessment.
Mask SSNs everywhere a full SSN isn’t operationally required.

details.description: The FTC Safeguards Rule requires a qualified individual, a written risk assessment, MFA, encryption, and vendor oversight. Gaps here block any new aid tooling.
implementationSteps: Name the qualified individual.
Complete a written risk assessment covering aid systems.
Enforce MFA and encryption for anyone accessing aid data.
Add safeguards language to vendor contracts.
keyBlockers: Shared responsibility between aid, IT, and compliance.
privacyNotes: Title IV participation obligates the institution to comply with GLBA safeguards. Findings can surface in federal audits.

nodes.label: Advising & Student Success
nodes.summary: Academic advising, coaching, and retention.

nodes.label: Academic Advisor
nodes.summary: Guides students through degree requirements and course selection.

details.context: Advisors field hundreds of repetitive questions each term about prerequisites, transfer credit, and graduation requirements, all governed by catalog rules that change yearly.
details.problemStatement: Students wait days for routine answers, and advisors have little time left for students at risk of leaving.

details.description: A student-facing assistant answers requirement questions from the catalog year the student entered under, and escalates anything ambiguous to a human advisor.
details.pattern: RAG over versioned policy documents, with escalation.
signals: Most questions are answerable from the published catalog.
Advisors keep a personal FAQ document.
implementationSteps: Index catalogs by year and program with explicit version metadata.
Launch in general-questions mode with no student records.
Later, add authenticated, degree-audit-aware answers once privacy review is complete.
Review a weekly sample of answers with advising leadership.
keyBlockers: Wrong answers about graduation carry real harm. Agree accuracy thresholds first.
privacyNotes: Phase 1, catalog only, uses public data.

Phase 2 reads the student’s degree audit. That requires SSO, access to the logged-in student’s own record only, a school-official agreement with the vendor, and no retention of conversations beyond what advising needs.
The contract must prohibit the vendor from using student data to train or improve its models, and must require deletion when the contract ends.

details.description: Degree rules exist as prose in PDFs and inconsistent degree-audit configuration, so no tool can reason over them reliably.
signals: The degree audit and the catalog disagree.
implementationSteps: Pick one program and encode its rules as structured requirements.
Reconcile them with the degree audit.
Make the registrar the owner of the structured version.
keyBlockers: Registrar capacity.
Curriculum changes land late in the cycle.

details.description: A shared note structure lets any advisor pick up a student’s history, and repeated questions become FAQ content.
implementationSteps: Define required fields: topic, outcome, follow-up.
Configure the CRM note template.
Review top topics monthly and publish FAQ updates.
keyBlockers: Advisors resist extra typing unless it saves time elsewhere.
privacyNotes: Notes in a shared advising system are education records, and students have the right to inspect them. The “sole possession” exclusion covers only private memory aids that are never shared.
Write factual, professional notes. Don’t record health or mental-health details; refer the student and note only that a referral happened.

nodes.label: Student Success Coach
nodes.summary: Proactively reaches students who show signs of struggling.

details.context: Warning signs such as LMS inactivity, missed assignments, holds, and midterm grades are spread across systems. Coaches learn about struggling students after withdrawal deadlines pass.
details.problemStatement: Outreach comes too late to change outcomes, and caseloads are too large to monitor manually.

details.description: A model scores retention risk from academic engagement signals to prioritize coach outreach. It prioritizes a human conversation; it does not label students.
implementationSteps: Use behavioral and academic signals, and exclude protected characteristics as features.
Audit for disparate impact across demographic groups before launch and each term.
Show coaches reasons, not just a score.
Never use scores for admissions, aid, or discipline decisions.
keyBlockers: Model bias and trust.
Needs integrated data (see gap).
privacyNotes: Scores are derived education records. Restrict them to coaches and advisors with legitimate educational interest.
Be transparent: tell students what data informs outreach.
Limit access to staff with a legitimate educational interest; role-based access should mirror the SIS security model.

details.description: A rule-based alert fires when a student has not logged in to any course for 7 days, or misses two assignments, and creates an outreach task for their coach.
implementationSteps: Define rules with faculty input.
Integrate LMS activity with the success CRM.
Track outreach and outcomes.
keyBlockers: Online and in-person courses use the LMS differently.
privacyNotes: Alerts go only to the assigned coach or advisor.
Outreach messages shouldn’t list specific grades in email subject lines or previews.

details.description: Every alert has one owner, a response deadline, and a documented close-out, so no student falls between offices.
implementationSteps: Define alert types and owners.
Set response SLAs.
Report closure rates monthly.
keyBlockers: Many offices, no single leader.
privacyNotes: Referrals to counseling or disability services should say only “referred.” Clinical or disability details stay in those offices’ separate systems.

details.description: LMS, SIS, and advising CRM data are not integrated, and there is no governance agreement on who may see combined profiles.
implementationSteps: Draft a data-sharing agreement with defined roles.
Build an integration with role-based views.
Document the data inventory.
keyBlockers: Data governance council approval.
privacyNotes: Combining data creates a more sensitive profile than any single source. Apply data minimization and log access.

nodes.label: Registrar & Records
nodes.summary: Official academic records, enrollment verification, and FERPA stewardship.

nodes.label: Records Specialist
nodes.summary: Handles transcripts, verifications, and records requests.

details.context: The office receives a steady stream of enrollment verifications, transcript orders, and records questions from students, employers, landlords, and parents.
details.problemStatement: Manual handling is slow, and every request is a chance to disclose something the requester shouldn’t receive.

details.description: Students generate official enrollment verifications themselves, and third parties verify through a clearinghouse or portal, with no staff handling.
implementationSteps: Enable student self-service in the SIS or clearinghouse.
Publish instructions for employers and insurers.
Retire the manual request form.
keyBlockers: Some requesters insist on custom letters.
privacyNotes: Automated disclosures must honor a student’s confidentiality (directory opt-out) flag.
Keep a record of non-consensual disclosures to third parties as required by 34 CFR 99.32.

details.description: A standard script and checklist for every records request: verify identity, check for a consent release or applicable exception, check confidentiality flags, and log the disclosure.
implementationSteps: Write the script for phone, email, and counter requests.
Use an online FERPA consent-release form students can manage.
Train staff yearly and require FERPA training before system access.
keyBlockers: High staff turnover in front-line roles.
privacyNotes: Parents have no automatic right to a college student’s records. Disclose only with the student’s written consent, or with documentation that the student is a tax dependent.
Treat urgency and authority claims from callers as red flags for social engineering.

details.description: Classify incoming emails by request type and route them to the right queue with a suggested template. Staff review and send every reply.
implementationSteps: Label a sample of past requests.
Classify into queues only. Never auto-send.
Measure routing accuracy.
keyBlockers: Emails contain student identifiers and sometimes documents.
privacyNotes: Run inside the institution’s email or ticketing platform under its existing data agreement.
Automated replies must never include record content. Identity must be verified first.

nodes.label: Student Affairs & Wellbeing
nodes.summary: Disability services, counseling, and student wellbeing.

nodes.label: Accessibility Services Coordinator
nodes.summary: Determines and coordinates academic accommodations.

details.context: Each term, coordinators generate accommodation letters for every registered student and every course, then answer faculty questions about implementing them.
details.problemStatement: Letters arrive late in the term, and documentation is handled through email and shared drives.

details.description: An accessibility management system generates course-specific letters from approved accommodations as soon as the student requests them, and delivers them to instructors through a secure portal.
implementationSteps: Adopt an accessibility management system that integrates with the SIS.
Let students request letters per course each term.
Have faculty acknowledge receipt in the portal.
keyBlockers: Procurement and SIS integration.
privacyNotes: Letters list accommodations only. Never include a diagnosis or disability type.
Faculty receive only what they need to implement the accommodation.

details.description: A tempting idea: summarize clinicians’ documentation to speed eligibility review. The diagnosis: not appropriate yet. The data is highly sensitive, the decisions are individualized, and the time saved is small compared to the risk.
details.pattern: Diagnosis: don’t automate. Fix the workflow first.
implementationSteps: Revisit only after secure document storage exists (see gap).
If ever piloted: private deployment only, the coordinator makes every determination, and students are informed.
keyBlockers: Health information in disability files is among the most sensitive data the institution holds.
Eligibility decisions must be individualized under the ADA.
privacyNotes: Disability documentation is an education record with heightened sensitivity. Some institutions also treat it under state health privacy laws.
Sending it to a general-purpose AI service is not acceptable.

details.description: Medical and psychological documentation is stored in inboxes and broadly shared folders, which blocks safe automation of anything else.
implementationSteps: Move documentation into the access-controlled accessibility system.
Purge copies from email and drives.
Set a records retention schedule.
keyBlockers: Historical files are scattered.
privacyNotes: Access should be limited to accessibility services staff. Other offices, including advising and faculty, get only accommodation outcomes.

nodes.label: Counseling Center Coordinator
nodes.summary: Manages intake and scheduling for student mental-health services.

details.context: Demand peaks around midterms and finals. Intake happens by phone, and waitlists live in spreadsheets.
details.problemStatement: Students wait weeks for a first appointment, and urgent needs can be missed in the queue.

details.description: Students book initial consultations online after a brief screening. Any screening that indicates risk triggers an immediate same-day clinician callback instead of a booking.
implementationSteps: Use the clinical EHR’s scheduling module.
Have clinicians define risk-screening rules.
Show crisis resources on every page.
keyBlockers: Clinical leadership approval of the screening rules.
privacyNotes: Counseling records live in a separate clinical system, never the SIS or advising CRM.
Reminders shouldn’t reveal the service. Use “You have an appointment at 2pm,” not “Counseling Center appointment,” in SMS and email.
Treatment records are excluded from FERPA’s education-records definition only while used solely for treatment. Once shared elsewhere they become education records, so don’t share them.

details.description: Match students to the right level of support (workshops, groups, single sessions, ongoing therapy) instead of routing everyone to weekly individual therapy.
implementationSteps: Define care levels and criteria.
Train intake staff.
Track wait times by level.
keyBlockers: Culture change for clinicians and students.

nodes.label: IT, Data & Institutional Research
nodes.summary: Enterprise systems, security, privacy, and institutional reporting.

nodes.label: Institutional Research Analyst
nodes.summary: Produces official statistics and analytics about students and outcomes.

details.context: IR produces IPEDS, state, and accreditation reports from SIS snapshots using a patchwork of queries and spreadsheets maintained by one or two people.
details.problemStatement: Reports are hard to reproduce, numbers shift between years, and knowledge walks out the door with staff.

details.description: Version-controlled queries run against frozen census snapshots, with automated checks against the prior year.
implementationSteps: Freeze census-date snapshots.
Move queries into version control.
Add automated year-over-year variance checks.
keyBlockers: Analyst time to refactor legacy queries.
privacyNotes: Snapshots contain unit-level education records. Restrict warehouse access to IR.
Published outputs must be aggregate, with small-cell suppression (for example, hide counts under 10) so individuals can’t be re-identified.

details.description: Offices define “enrolled,” “full-time,” and “first-generation” differently, so numbers never reconcile.
implementationSteps: Publish a data dictionary.
Get sign-off from data stewards.
Tag every report with the definitions it uses.
keyBlockers: Politically sensitive numbers.

details.description: Named data stewards per domain approve definitions, access, and data-sharing requests.
implementationSteps: Charter the council.
Name stewards per domain.
Create an access request workflow.
keyBlockers: Executive sponsorship.

nodes.label: IT Security & Privacy Officer
nodes.summary: Protects institutional data and reviews technology for risk.

details.context: Faculty and staff request dozens of new AI tools a term, from writing assistants to meeting transcription, often after they have already started using them.
details.problemStatement: Reviews are ad hoc and slow, so people bypass them and student data ends up in unvetted services.

details.description: Publish a simple data classification (public, internal, FERPA, restricted) and a list showing which tools are approved for which class.
implementationSteps: Adopt four data classes with examples.
Map approved tools to the highest class each may handle.
Publish it where faculty will actually see it, including the LMS and the faculty portal.
keyBlockers: Keeping the list current.
privacyNotes: This is the backbone that makes every other outcome in this atlas safe to act on.

details.description: Standard vendor contracts and click-through terms don’t designate the vendor as a school official, restrict data use, or prohibit model training.
implementationSteps: Create a student-data addendum template.
Require it for any tool touching FERPA-class data.
Include breach notification, deletion, and subprocessor disclosure.
keyBlockers: Large vendors resist custom terms.
Click-through consumer terms can’t be negotiated.
privacyNotes: A vendor processing education records must qualify under FERPA’s school-official exception: it performs an institutional function, stays under the institution’s direct control, and uses records only for that purpose (34 CFR 99.31(a)(1)).
The contract must prohibit the vendor from using student data to train or improve its models, and must require deletion when the contract ends.
Individual employees generally can’t accept click-through terms that bind the institution to share student data.

details.description: A single intake form routes requests to privacy, security, accessibility, and procurement reviewers in parallel, with a published turnaround time.
implementationSteps: Build the form, asking which data class the tool will touch.
Auto-route by data class, with light review for public data.
Publish decisions to the approved-tools list.
keyBlockers: Reviewer capacity.

nodes.label: Library
nodes.summary: Research help, instruction, and collections.

nodes.label: Reference & Instruction Librarian
nodes.summary: Helps students and faculty find and evaluate sources.

details.context: Students do most of their research at night, while reference desk hours end in the early evening.
details.problemStatement: Students give up or rely on low-quality sources when help isn’t available.

details.description: An assistant helps students form search strategies and finds items in the library catalog and databases, with a handoff to a librarian.
implementationSteps: Ground it in the discovery layer and research guides.
Teach search strategy rather than just returning answers.
Offer a “talk to a librarian” handoff.
keyBlockers: Database vendor terms for AI access.
privacyNotes: Library patron records and search histories are confidential under most state library laws, and may also be education records. Don’t tie chat logs to student identity, and set short retention.
Don’t allow the vendor to use queries for profiling or model training.

details.description: Join a cooperative chat service where librarians across institutions staff overnight shifts.
implementationSteps: Join the consortium service.
Contribute staffing hours.
Share local FAQs with partner librarians.
keyBlockers: Local knowledge gaps among partner librarians.
privacyNotes: Confirm the consortium’s chat transcript retention and privacy terms match local policy.

nodes.label: Healthcare
nodes.summary: Hospitals, clinics, and health systems: clinical care, behavioral health, revenue cycle, and patient access.

nodes.label: Clinical Care
nodes.summary: Physicians, advanced practice providers, and nursing.

nodes.label: Physician / APP
nodes.summary: Physicians and advanced practice providers in ambulatory and inpatient care.

details.context: Clinicians spend one to two hours a day after clinic finishing notes in the EHR. This after-hours charting is a leading driver of burnout.
details.problemStatement: Documentation crowds out patient care and rest, and rushed notes reduce accuracy and coding quality.

details.description: With the patient’s consent, capture the visit conversation and generate a draft note in the clinic’s format for the clinician to review, edit, and sign.
details.pattern: Speech-to-text plus structured summarization, with clinician sign-off.
signals: Notes are mostly narrative history and assessment/plan.
implementationSteps: Pilot in specialties with conversational visits.
Integrate drafts into the EHR note workflow, not a separate app.
Measure after-hours EHR time before and after.
Script patient consent, with an easy opt-out.
keyBlockers: Vendor security review and BAA.
A draft that omits or invents findings creates liability, so every note needs clinician review.
privacyNotes: Any vendor that stores or processes PHI must sign a business associate agreement, and the contract should bar using PHI to train its models.
Get consent to record, and follow the strictest state recording-consent law that applies.
Set a short retention period for audio, and delete it once the note is signed unless policy requires otherwise.
Exclude or pause for sensitive visits (for example, SUD treatment or psychotherapy) unless those are explicitly in scope.

details.description: Replace free-form notes with specialty-specific smart templates and shared phrase libraries. This cuts clicks without any new technology.
implementationSteps: Shadow three clinicians to find repeated text.
Build templates with required fields only.
Retire unused legacy templates.
keyBlockers: EHR build-team backlog.
Template sprawl if not governed.

nodes.label: No Approved Pathway for PHI in AI Tools

details.description: There is no approved way to send PHI to an AI service, so clinicians either do without or paste PHI into consumer tools. That is a reportable HIPAA breach risk.
implementationSteps: Stand up an AI governance committee with privacy, security, clinical, and equity members.
Define vendor criteria: BAA, data retention, no model training on PHI.
Approve at least one reference architecture so there is a sanctioned option.
keyBlockers: Executive sponsorship.
Legal review timelines.
privacyNotes: Pasting PHI into a tool without a BAA is an impermissible disclosure and may trigger breach notification.
Clinical decision-support uses also need a bias review under Section 1557.

details.context: Patient portal messages have surged. Physicians answer questions about results, refills, and symptoms, often after hours and unpaid.
details.problemStatement: Replies are slow, clinicians burn out, and routine requests reach the physician when another team member could handle them.

details.description: The EHR drafts a reply grounded in the patient’s chart. The clinician edits and sends it, and nothing goes out automatically.
implementationSteps: Enable within the EHR vendor’s environment under the existing BAA.
Start with lower-risk message types such as refills and logistics.
Track edit rates and clinician-reported safety issues.
keyBlockers: Drafts can sound confident while being clinically wrong.
Decide in policy whether to tell patients that AI helped draft replies.
privacyNotes: Keep processing inside the EHR’s contracted environment.
Under information-blocking rules, results are often released to the portal before the clinician has reviewed them, which drives much of the message volume. Drafting must not delay that release.
Don’t let drafts pull in sensitive history (SUD, psychotherapy, reproductive or HIV care) that the question doesn’t need.

nodes.label: Message Routing to Care Team Pools

details.description: Rules route refill, scheduling, and form requests to nurse or staff pools, so physicians see only messages that need them.
implementationSteps: Categorize a month of messages.
Configure routing rules and pool ownership.
Monitor turnaround by pool.
keyBlockers: Patients choose the wrong category, so rules need a manual reroute path.
privacyNotes: Pool members get access based on their role; audit access to high-profile or employee patients.

details.description: Standing protocols let RNs and MAs resolve common requests, such as normal results or refills within parameters, without the physician.
implementationSteps: Write protocols with physician leadership.
Train and credential staff.
Audit a sample monthly.
keyBlockers: Scope-of-practice rules vary by state.

nodes.label: Nurse Manager
nodes.summary: Runs unit staffing, scheduling, and quality.

details.context: Managers build schedules in spreadsheets and fill last-minute callouts by texting staff one by one.
details.problemStatement: Gaps are found late, and filling them costs hours of manager time and expensive agency shifts.

details.description: When a callout is logged, eligible staff are notified automatically, and the first acceptance is assigned within overtime rules.
implementationSteps: Encode eligibility rules: credential, unit, hours worked.
Connect the scheduling system’s callout event to an SMS workflow.
Write acceptances back to the schedule.
keyBlockers: Union agreements may set the order in which shifts are offered.
privacyNotes: Staff data is employee PII, not PHI. Store only “unavailable,” never the medical or family reason for a callout.

details.description: License and certification expirations live in HR while schedules live elsewhere, so automated assignment could schedule ineligible staff.
implementationSteps: Feed credential expirations into scheduling.
Block assignment when a credential has expired.
keyBlockers: HR system API access.

nodes.label: Behavioral Health
nodes.summary: Mental health and substance use disorder (SUD) treatment.

nodes.label: SUD Counselor / BH Clinician
nodes.summary: Provides substance use and mental health treatment.

details.context: Patients in the SUD program also see primary care and visit the ED, but SUD records are kept separate under 42 CFR Part 2.
details.problemStatement: Care is fragmented. Unsure what they may share, staff often share nothing, even when the patient would consent.

details.description: Use a standard, plain-language consent that patients can sign once for treatment, payment, and health care operations, plus training on what it allows.
implementationSteps: Adopt a single-consent form reviewed by counsel.
Build it into intake, and let patients revoke it.
Train staff on the redisclosure notice that must go with disclosures.
keyBlockers: Staff fear of getting it wrong.
privacyNotes: The 2024 Part 2 rule allows one consent for all future treatment, payment, and operations uses. Uses against the patient in legal proceedings still require consent or a court order.
Records disclosed under Part 2 must carry the required redisclosure notice.

details.description: The EHR can’t tag and filter Part 2 records, so sharing is all-or-nothing and staff default to nothing.
implementationSteps: Inventory where SUD data lives: notes, problem list, medications.
Enable data-segmentation features or a separate compartment.
Test what flows out through HIE and portal feeds.
keyBlockers: EHR vendor capability.
privacyNotes: Medication lists alone can reveal SUD treatment (for example, buprenorphine), so segmentation must cover more than notes.

nodes.label: AI Summaries of Therapy & SUD Notes

details.description: The idea is to summarize therapy and SUD notes for other clinicians. The diagnosis: not yet. The data carries the strictest protections and segmentation doesn’t exist, so summaries would leak protected content into general records.
details.pattern: Diagnosis: fix consent and segmentation first.
implementationSteps: Revisit once segmentation and consent workflows are in place.
If piloted: private deployment, summaries stay within the program, and clinicians review them.
keyBlockers: Psychotherapy notes need separate patient authorization for most uses under HIPAA.
privacyNotes: A summary is a new disclosure. It inherits Part 2 and psychotherapy-note restrictions and must not flow into the general chart.

nodes.label: Revenue Cycle
nodes.summary: Billing, coding, claims, and prior authorization.

nodes.label: Billing Specialist
nodes.summary: Works claims from submission through payment or appeal.

details.context: Many claims are denied on first submission. Specialists work each one by reading remittance codes, pulling documentation, and writing appeals.
details.problemStatement: Denials pile up faster than they are worked, and many are written off when the appeal window closes.

details.description: Classify denials by root cause and expected recovery, then draft appeal letters citing documentation and payer policy.
implementationSteps: Label past denials with their outcomes.
Prioritize by expected recovery.
Generate appeal drafts for specialist review.
keyBlockers: Payer policies change frequently.
privacyNotes: Any vendor that stores or processes PHI must sign a business associate agreement, and the contract should bar using PHI to train its models.
Pull only the chart excerpts the appeal needs (minimum necessary), not the whole record.

details.description: Parse 835 remittance files from the clearinghouse automatically, and route denials into work queues by reason code.
implementationSteps: Subscribe to clearinghouse 835 delivery.
Map CARC/RARC codes to queues.
Track denial rates by payer and reason.
keyBlockers: Clearinghouse setup.
privacyNotes: 835/837 files are HIPAA standard transactions containing PHI. Use secure transfer and restrict the landing folders.

details.description: A weekly cross-functional review of top denial reasons, fixing them upstream at registration and coding.
implementationSteps: Pull the top 10 reasons weekly.
Assign an upstream owner to each.
Trend the rate over time.
keyBlockers: Front desk and coding report to different leaders.

details.context: Staff submit prior authorizations through payer portals, fax, and phone, then chase status manually.
details.problemStatement: Authorizations delay care and consume staff time, and most of the work is re-entering information already in the chart.

nodes.label: Electronic Prior Authorization via Payer APIs

details.description: Use payer prior authorization APIs from the EHR to check requirements, submit, and track decisions without portals or fax.
implementationSteps: Inventory payers by API readiness.
Automate the top payers first.
Keep a manual path for the rest.
keyBlockers: Payer API rollout follows the CMS timeline, and commercial plans outside the rule may lag.
privacyNotes: Send only the clinical data the payer’s criteria require.

details.description: Draft the clinical justification by mapping relevant chart history to the payer’s criteria, for staff review.
implementationSteps: Collect criteria for the top 20 procedures.
Generate criteria-mapped summaries.
Staff review before submission.
keyBlockers: Criteria are often not published in a usable format.
privacyNotes: Any vendor that stores or processes PHI must sign a business associate agreement, and the contract should bar using PHI to train its models.

nodes.label: Patient Access
nodes.summary: Scheduling, registration, and reminders.

nodes.label: Patient Access Representative
nodes.summary: Schedules appointments and registers patients.

details.context: Some clinics lose a large share of slots to no-shows while new patients wait weeks for an appointment.
details.problemStatement: Wasted capacity and long waits, which fall hardest on patients facing transportation, work, or childcare barriers.

details.description: Two-way SMS reminders let patients confirm or cancel, and cancelled slots are offered automatically to waitlisted patients.
implementationSteps: Enable two-way reminders in the scheduling system.
Offer freed slots to the waitlist automatically.
Track fill rate.
keyBlockers: Patient contact data quality.
privacyNotes: Keep texts minimal: time and location only. No diagnosis, and no department name that reveals sensitive care (for example “Oncology” or “Behavioral Health”).
Honor patients’ communication preferences and TCPA consent.

details.description: Predict which appointments are at risk and offer support, such as a ride, a telehealth switch, or a reminder call. Don’t double-book those patients.
implementationSteps: Train on scheduling history.
Audit the model for disparate impact by race, language, and payer.
Use scores to trigger outreach, not to overbook.
keyBlockers: Overbooking by risk score punishes the patients with the most barriers.
privacyNotes: Under Section 1557, covered entities must identify and mitigate discrimination risk in patient care decision support tools.
Leave out features that proxy for protected characteristics unless the goal is to measure bias.

details.description: Hold a share of each day open for same-day and next-day visits. Shorter lead times reduce no-shows.
implementationSteps: Analyze lead time against no-show rate.
Redesign templates.
Review monthly.
keyBlockers: Provider preference for fully booked schedules.

nodes.label: Police Department
nodes.summary: Municipal and county law enforcement: patrol, records, investigations, and 911 communications.

nodes.label: Patrol Operations
nodes.summary: Uniformed patrol and field supervision.

nodes.label: Patrol Officer
nodes.summary: Responds to calls for service and documents incidents.

details.context: Officers spend a large share of each shift writing reports, often from memory, hours after the call. Body-worn cameras record most interactions.
details.problemStatement: Report writing takes officers off the street, quality varies, and supervisors and prosecutors send reports back for missing elements.

nodes.label: AI Report Drafts from Body-Cam Audio

details.description: Generate a first-draft narrative from the body-worn camera transcript. The officer corrects it, adds their own observations, and attests to it.
details.pattern: AI drafting with mandatory officer review and attestation.
implementationSteps: Get prosecutor and defense-bar input before piloting.
Require officers to edit and attest, and flag any placeholders left unedited.
Label reports as AI-assisted and retain drafts where state law requires.
Audit a sample against the video.
keyBlockers: A hallucinated detail can undermine a prosecution and an officer’s credibility.
Prosecutors may decline AI-drafted reports.
privacyNotes: Any vendor with access to criminal justice information must meet the CJIS Security Policy and sign the CJIS Security Addendum. Most consumer and general-purpose AI services don’t.
Drafts and AI outputs may be discoverable under Brady/Giglio. Keep them under the records retention policy.
Transcripts can capture victims, juveniles, and bystanders, so exclude or restrict sensitive incident types.

details.description: Incident-type templates list the elements needed to charge each offense, so reports are complete the first time.
implementationSteps: Work with prosecutors on the elements per offense.
Build templates into the RMS.
Track the return rate.
keyBlockers: RMS configuration effort.

nodes.label: RMS Not Integrated with CAD & Video

details.description: Officers retype times, locations, and names from CAD, and the RMS can’t link to video, so any drafting tool has little structured data to work from.
implementationSteps: Prefill RMS from CAD.
Link evidence IDs from the video system.
Standardize name and location records.
keyBlockers: Vendor integration costs.
privacyNotes: Integrations move CJI between systems, and each connection must meet CJIS encryption and audit requirements.

nodes.label: Patrol Sergeant
nodes.summary: Supervises patrol officers and reviews their conduct.

details.context: The department records thousands of hours of video, but supervisors review only a sliver, usually after a complaint.
details.problemStatement: Coaching opportunities and policy problems surface late, if at all.

details.description: Analyze transcripts for markers such as use-of-force language or escalation, and queue those clips for supervisor review and coaching.
implementationSteps: Agree on what gets flagged and how it is used, with labor representatives.
Emphasize coaching over discipline for most flags.
Measure false flags.
keyBlockers: Union agreements.
Trust that the tool is fair.
privacyNotes: Any vendor with access to criminal justice information must meet the CJIS Security Policy and sign the CJIS Security Addendum. Most consumer and general-purpose AI services don’t.
Footage often shows victims, minors, medical situations, and home interiors, so access must be role-restricted and audited.
Don’t add face recognition. Analyze transcripts only.

details.description: Each sergeant reviews a random set of videos per officer each month against defined criteria, and feeds coaching into training.
implementationSteps: Define the review rubric.
Randomize selection.
Track coaching themes department-wide.
keyBlockers: Sergeant time.

nodes.label: Records & Public Information
nodes.summary: Records management, releases, and retention.

nodes.label: Records Clerk
nodes.summary: Processes records requests and releases.

details.context: Requests for reports and video arrive under state public records law, with statutory deadlines. Redacting video is frame-by-frame work.
details.problemStatement: Backlogs, missed deadlines, and lawsuits, plus the risk of releasing a victim’s or juvenile’s identity.

details.description: Detect faces, plates, screens, and spoken names for redaction, followed by a mandatory human quality check before release.
implementationSteps: Run it in a CJIS-compliant environment.
Require human QA on every release.
Log each redaction and its legal basis.
keyBlockers: Detection misses in low light or crowded scenes.
privacyNotes: One missed juvenile face or victim name can cause serious harm, so a human must check every release.
Withholding rules differ by state. Encode them in redaction templates rather than relying on memory.

details.description: A portal logs requests, calculates statutory deadlines, and releases routine records automatically where the law allows.
implementationSteps: Adopt a request-tracking portal.
Configure deadlines by record type.
Publish frequently requested records proactively.
keyBlockers: Procurement.
privacyNotes: Requester identities may themselves be protected. Check state law.

details.description: Video and reports are kept indefinitely or purged inconsistently, which raises storage cost, discovery burden, and breach exposure.
implementationSteps: Map categories to the state retention schedule.
Configure automatic retention in the evidence system.
Apply legal holds for pending cases.
keyBlockers: Fear of deleting something needed later.
privacyNotes: Keeping data beyond its retention period increases what a breach exposes.

nodes.label: Investigations
nodes.summary: Detectives and crime analysis.

nodes.label: Detective
nodes.summary: Investigates cases and prepares them for prosecution.

details.context: A single case can involve phone extractions, CCTV, social media returns, and hours of interviews, often terabytes of data.
details.problemStatement: Investigators can’t review everything, and exculpatory evidence may be missed.

details.description: Transcribe, index, and search seized material, with timestamped links back to the source. Investigators verify everything the tool surfaces.
implementationSteps: Deploy on-premises or in a CJIS-compliant cloud.
Restrict searches to the data and date ranges the warrant authorizes.
Log every query for later review.
keyBlockers: Defense challenges to AI-assisted review.
privacyNotes: Search must stay within the warrant’s scope. The tool must not become a way to search beyond it.
Anything the tool surfaces, including exculpatory hits, may need to be disclosed.
No vendor model training on case data.

details.description: Ingest evidence with automatic hashing and chain-of-custody logging, and share it with prosecutors through the system instead of on USB drives.
implementationSteps: Adopt a DEMS.
Integrate with the RMS and prosecutor’s office.
Retire physical media sharing.
keyBlockers: Storage cost.
privacyNotes: Access logs are part of the chain of custody. Keep them tamper-evident.

nodes.label: Crime Analyst
nodes.summary: Analyzes crime patterns to inform deployment.

details.context: Command staff want tools that predict where and by whom crime will occur, and vendors are pitching predictive policing products.
details.problemStatement: The department is under pressure to adopt tools whose bias, accuracy, and legal risk are poorly understood.

details.description: The diagnosis: not recommended. Person-based risk lists learn from historical enforcement patterns, can amplify bias, and several agencies have abandoned them.
details.pattern: Diagnosis: don’t build it. Invest in place-based analysis and prevention.
implementationSteps: Decline person-based scoring.
Redirect toward place-based analysis with transparent methods.
keyBlockers: Legal and community-trust risk outweighs claimed benefit.
privacyNotes: Putting people into intelligence systems without reasonable suspicion violates 28 CFR Part 23 for federally funded systems.
Lists derived from arrests reflect where enforcement happened, not only where crime occurred.

details.description: Automated weekly crime-pattern dashboards from RMS and CAD, with a public-facing version.
implementationSteps: Automate extracts from the RMS.
Publish aggregate public dashboards.
Document the methodology.
keyBlockers: Data quality in RMS offense codes.
privacyNotes: Geomask locations, especially for domestic violence and sexual assault, so victims can’t be located.

details.description: Before acquiring any analytics or surveillance tool: a public use policy, community input, and an annual audit of use and impact.
implementationSteps: Draft a use-policy template.
Hold a public comment period.
Publish an annual audit.
keyBlockers: Slower procurement.

nodes.label: Emergency Communications (911)
nodes.summary: Call-taking and dispatch.

nodes.label: 911 Telecommunicator
nodes.summary: Answers emergency and non-emergency calls and dispatches units.

details.context: Understaffed dispatch centers handle large volumes of non-emergency calls, such as noise, parking, and report requests, on the same staff as 911.
details.problemStatement: 911 answer times slip, and staff burn out.

nodes.label: AI Agent for Non-Emergency Lines Only

details.description: A voice agent answers the non-emergency line, takes minor reports, and routes callers. Any sign of an emergency transfers the call to a human immediately.
implementationSteps: Never deploy on 911 lines.
Define immediate human-transfer triggers.
Review transcripts weekly.
keyBlockers: Missing an emergency that was misclassified as non-emergency.
privacyNotes: Tell callers they are talking to an automated system, and that calls are recorded.
Transcripts become records. Apply retention and CJIS controls to them.

details.description: Residents file minor property-crime and lost-property reports online, and records staff review them before they are entered in the RMS.
implementationSteps: Choose eligible report types.
Deploy the online form.
Route submissions to records staff.
keyBlockers: Residents expecting an in-person response.
privacyNotes: Collect only what the report needs, and use encrypted transmission.

details.description: Triage protocols route behavioral-health calls to crisis teams or 988 where appropriate, freeing officers and getting callers better help.
implementationSteps: Define call types that are eligible.
Build a handoff protocol with the crisis team.
Track outcomes.
keyBlockers: Crisis team availability, especially overnight.
privacyNotes: Share only the minimum health information the crisis team needs. Crisis providers may be HIPAA-covered once they receive it.

nodes.label: Maritime
nodes.summary: Shipping companies, vessel operations, and ports and terminals.

nodes.label: Vessel Operations
nodes.summary: Shipboard engineering, navigation, and crew.

nodes.label: Chief Engineer
nodes.summary: Responsible for propulsion, machinery, and maintenance aboard.

details.context: Vessels run a planned maintenance system under the ISM Code, mostly on calendar or running-hour intervals, far from shore support and spare parts.
details.problemStatement: Developing faults are missed between intervals, and an unplanned failure at sea means off-hire time, safety risk, and costly emergency repairs.

details.description: Anomaly detection on engine and machinery sensor data flags developing faults so work can be scheduled before a failure.
implementationSteps: Start with one critical system, such as main engine or purifiers.
Historize sensor data aboard and sync summaries ashore.
Feed confirmed alerts into the maintenance system as work orders.
keyBlockers: Sensor coverage (see gap).
Satellite bandwidth.
privacyNotes: Connecting shipboard operational technology to shore creates cyber risk. Use one-way data flows or segmented networks, and address it in the safety management system.

details.description: Sensor readings appear on alarm panels but aren’t stored, so there is no history to learn from.
implementationSteps: Install a data logger on key systems.
Agree on a data model across the fleet.
Budget bandwidth for data sync.
keyBlockers: Older vessels lack digital sensors.

details.description: Standard failure codes and required findings when closing each maintenance job, so recurring problems become visible across the fleet.
implementationSteps: Adopt a failure-code list.
Make findings mandatory on close-out.
Hold a quarterly fleet review.
keyBlockers: Crew time during port calls.

nodes.label: Master / Deck Officer
nodes.summary: Commands the vessel and handles port-call formalities.

details.context: Each port call requires crew and passenger lists, advance notice of arrival, customs, health, and security declarations, often submitted separately to different authorities and agents.
details.problemStatement: Officers retype the same data for every port, and errors lead to delays, fines, or denied entry.

nodes.label: Submit Once via Maritime Single Window

details.description: Generate standard FAL forms from one crew and voyage data source, and submit them through the port’s national single window.
implementationSteps: Keep one master crew list per vessel, synced with the crewing office.
Generate FAL-standard data sets.
Integrate with single windows at frequently visited ports.
keyBlockers: Single-window formats still vary by country.
privacyNotes: Crew lists contain passport numbers, dates of birth, and nationality. Submit only through official channels, not by email to multiple agents.
Where GDPR applies, crew data needs a lawful basis, retention limits, and processor agreements with agents.

details.description: Extract data from passports, seafarer IDs, and STCW certificates to fill crew records and flag certificates about to expire.
implementationSteps: Process ashore in the crewing system, not on personal devices.
Verify extracted fields.
Alert on expiring certificates.
keyBlockers: Document formats vary by flag state.
privacyNotes: Passport and ID images are high-risk personal data. Store them encrypted, restrict access, and use a processor agreement with any vendor.

details.description: Each vessel keeps its own crew spreadsheets, which drift from the crewing office’s records, so automated submission would propagate errors.
implementationSteps: Name one system of record for crew data.
Sync it with vessels at every crew change.
Delete stale local copies.
keyBlockers: Connectivity and crew-change turnover.
privacyNotes: Every stale copy is another place personal data can leak from.

details.context: MLC 2006 and STCW set minimum rest hours, and port state control inspects rest records. Port calls and drills compress schedules.
details.problemStatement: Records are often filled in afterwards to look compliant, which hides real fatigue risk and invites deficiencies.

details.description: Plan work and watches in a tool that warns before a schedule would break rest rules, and record actual hours as they happen.
implementationSteps: Adopt a tool that encodes MLC and STCW rules.
Plan port-call work in advance.
Review exceptions with the master.
keyBlockers: A culture of adjusting records after the fact.
privacyNotes: Rest records are personal data. Use them for safety and compliance, not as covert performance surveillance, and say so to crews.

details.description: Redesign watch rotations and port-call work plans, adding shore support where needed so rest rules can be kept honestly.
implementationSteps: Analyze actual work during port calls.
Adjust rotations.
Add shore or riding-crew support for peak periods.
keyBlockers: Crew cost.

nodes.label: Ports & Terminals
nodes.summary: Terminal operations and port facility security.

nodes.label: Terminal Operations Planner
nodes.summary: Plans berths, cranes, and yard space.

details.context: Vessels frequently arrive off-schedule. Planners juggle berth windows, crane gangs, and yard space from carrier emails and phone calls.
details.problemStatement: Late ETA changes leave cranes idle and ships waiting at anchor, burning fuel and adding emissions.

details.description: Predict arrival times from AIS positions, weather, and port congestion, and update the berth plan automatically.
implementationSteps: Ingest AIS and weather feeds.
Train on historical arrivals.
Show predicted versus declared ETA to planners.
keyBlockers: Carrier schedule data quality.
privacyNotes: AIS positions are broadcast publicly, but carrier commercial data needs data-sharing agreements.

details.description: Agree with carriers to slow-steam toward a confirmed berth time instead of racing to wait at anchor.
implementationSteps: Pilot with one carrier service.
Share berth availability early.
Measure anchorage time and fuel saved.
keyBlockers: Charter-party terms that reward arriving early.

nodes.label: Facility Security Officer
nodes.summary: Implements the port facility security plan.

details.context: Truck and personnel gates require credential verification for secure areas, and queues back up at peak times.
details.problemStatement: Manual checks are slow and error-prone, creating both congestion and security gaps.

details.description: Electronic credential readers and a truck appointment system verify access automatically, and exceptions go to guards.
implementationSteps: Deploy readers at secure-area entry points.
Integrate with the appointment system.
Define a manual fallback.
keyBlockers: Reader hardware in harsh environments.
privacyNotes: Credential reads and access logs are personal data and security records. Set retention and restrict access.

details.description: Detect perimeter intrusions and unattended objects from existing cameras, without identifying individuals.
implementationSteps: Use detection only, with no face recognition.
Tune for false alarms caused by weather and wildlife.
Route alerts to the security desk.
keyBlockers: High false-alarm rates at waterfront sites.
privacyNotes: Camera layouts and coverage gaps are security-sensitive information. Share them only with vendors who have a need to know.
Facial recognition triggers biometric privacy laws in some states. Avoid it.

nodes.label: Security Plan Lacks a Cyber Annex

details.description: The facility security plan predates connected gate systems and cameras, and has no cybersecurity plan as the new rule requires.
implementationSteps: Designate a cybersecurity officer.
Assess connected systems.
Write and submit the cybersecurity plan.
keyBlockers: Specialist cyber skills are scarce at terminals.
privacyNotes: Security and cybersecurity plans are SSI. Mark them, control access, and never paste them into general-purpose AI tools.

nodes.label: Fleet Performance & Compliance
nodes.summary: Shore-side fleet management, emissions, and environmental compliance.

nodes.label: Fleet Performance / Emissions Manager
nodes.summary: Monitors fuel, emissions, and carbon-intensity ratings.

details.context: Vessels report fuel consumption and emissions to IMO DCS, EU MRV and ETS, and CII ratings, mostly from manually typed noon reports and bunker delivery notes.
details.problemStatement: Errors and mismatches between regimes risk verifier rejections, penalties, and wrong EU ETS allowance purchases.

details.description: Replace emailed spreadsheets with validated digital noon reports that feed MRV, DCS, and CII calculations automatically.
implementationSteps: Adopt a digital reporting tool with range checks.
Integrate with the verifier’s submission.
Reconcile against bunker delivery notes.
keyBlockers: Crew adoption.

nodes.label: AI Anomaly Checks on Fuel Data

details.description: Flag implausible fuel, distance, or speed entries against vessel models and weather before submission.
implementationSteps: Build vessel performance baselines.
Flag outliers for the vessel to confirm.
Track the correction rate.
keyBlockers: Baseline quality on older vessels.

details.description: Consumption comes from tank soundings, so reported emissions, and the carbon cost that follows, are uncertain.
implementationSteps: Prioritize flow meters on high-consumption vessels.
Update the monitoring plan.
Calibrate meters against soundings.
keyBlockers: Capital cost and dry-dock timing.
